days.title: slot-3 branch trial, validation of 0.7.1, pipelining plan
findings: A third-slot conditional branch does not pay: it moves branches from the start of a group to the end of the previous one, but a branch at the start of a group already folds its target into the second slot, so the clock count barely changes (+0.4% DMIPS/MHz). Dropped.

The independent review of 0.7.1 found no bug in the committed design but a missing test: allowing a multiply to pair (the pre-0.7.1 rule) puts a store on the bus early, and the regression did not notice. The test is now in the regression and catches it.

Absolute performance, not DMIPS/MHz, decides the next steps: 0.3.0 reaches 22.49 MHz on ECP5 (about 21 DMIPS), with 79% of its critical path in routing. A pipelining plan was drafted (below); its figures are estimates until measured.

timeline.text: Candidate 0.7.2 written: conditional branch in the third slot (compare on the third slot's operands, target `pc3 + imm`, taken target misaligned does not issue there; the group's successor is the branch's outcome). New tests `triple_branch`, `triple_branch_misaligned`. Testbench `tb_core.sv` now counts second-slot, third-slot and third-slot-branch retirements on its DONE line, and `test_cpu.py` checks that `dual_issue_fold` and `triple_issue` use their slot (default caches, no wait cycles)
Regression: 52 programs x 3 wait patterns = 156 runs pass with default caches (15.7 s) and with 2-line caches (11.8 s); `triple_branch` retires 2 branches from the third slot
Unlogged Dhrystone run on the candidate (`rv64imb`, reference runtime, `-NoDevlog`): 2.2250 DMIPS/MHz, 255.8 clocks per run against 256.8 (-0.4%)

Blocker count on the candidate's trace (a scratch script groups the measured profile trace into issue groups): pairs stopped by a third-slot branch fell from 36.0 to 3.0 per run, but pairs stopped by a third-slot store rose from 18.0 to 48.0; triples rose by only 1.0 per run. The branch used to start the next group and fold its target into the second slot; now that target starts a group of its own. Candidate reverted; tests kept as plain differential tests

Independent validation of 0.7.1 by a review agent in a separate worktree at `c1b113f`: regression 150/150 (14.1 s) and 150/150 with 2-line caches (12.3 s); `check_bitmanip.py` passes (6.3 s, 28 B instructions, 33,124 and 15,003 retired); visualizer lessons pass after a rebuild (15.9 s); `check_repo.py` passes; RTL hashes, `cpu/VERSION`, tag and the 0.7.1 run rows agree with the records. No bug found in the multiply path. Mutants: reverting the pairing rule (`!m_op` to `!is_div`) passed the whole regression; three other multiply mutants were caught. Its focused scratch test caught the first. Tools: Icarus Verilog 12.0, Python 3.12.3 (WSL) and 3.12.10 (Windows), clang 18.1.3 (WSL) and 23.1.5 (Windows)

Review follow-ups: new tests `mul_then_store_pad0`, `mul_then_store_pad1` (a store after each multiply kind) and `mul_into_x0`; regression 55 programs x 3 = 165 runs pass with default and 2-line caches; with the pairing mutant applied, `mul_then_store_pad1` fails at event 14 (a store's W line before the multiply's R line). `runlog.py` no longer strips the leading space of `git status` output, which had cut the first character from the first dirty file name in run logs (for example "`EVLOG.md`"). `cpu/architecture.md` now lists the DIVIDE and MULTIPLY states and excludes multiplies from first-slot pairing in its text. Also reported: `cpu/programs-verification.json` and `cpu/visualizer-verification.json` still hold the RTL hashes of the initial commit (the regenerated copies in the working tree are current), and `cpu/dhrystone-rv64im-fastrt-results.json` is still the 0.6.0 run

Pipelining plan drafted by a planning agent from the RTL and the measurements: five short stages (PC, cache read, decode and register read, execute, memory and retire), instruction and data caches in block RAM, register file in LUT RAM (two copies for two read ports; a live-value table for two-wide), forwarding from two registered stages, static then BTB prediction, two-wide issue at most (slot 3 dropped), traps acted on at retirement. Estimates, not measurements: single-issue pipeline about 0.8 DMIPS/MHz at 60 to 75 MHz; two-wide about 1.3 DMIPS/MHz at 50 to 60 MHz (65 to 80 DMIPS, against about 21 for 0.3.0)
ECP5 synthesis of 0.7.0 and 0.7.1 still running after 30 minutes in Yosys `synth_ecp5` (0.3.0 took 59.5 s)
Commit `15074b8`: multiply-pairing and slot-use tests, slot-3 branch trial record, `runlog.py` fix

Pipeline what-if model `sim/cpu/bench/pipeline_model.py` (written by a side agent; Python 3.12.10) replayed the measured Dhrystone traces through an in-order pipeline with configurable prediction, width and stalls (instruction and data caches assumed to hit; redirect from E costs 3 bubbles, from D 2). Note: the `rv64imb` trace it read came from the reverted slot-3 branch candidate (255.8 clocks per run, against 256.8 for 0.7.1). `rv64imb` reference, clocks per run: single issue, not-taken 858.1 (0.663 DMIPS/MHz); static 813.1 (0.700); 64-entry BTB with a 4-entry return stack 639.3 (0.890); perfect prediction 579.1 (0.983); two-wide with a 64-entry BTB 465.2 (1.223); two-wide with perfect prediction 405.1 (1.405). Branch handling is the largest lever (about 279 of 858 clocks are control penalties without prediction); two-wide issue saves 145 to 175. Break-even: even two-wide with perfect prediction needs 1.58x the clocks of the measured core, single issue with a 64-entry BTB 2.50x, so a pipeline only wins if its clock is that much faster. Command: `python -B sim/cpu/bench/pipeline_model.py` plus sensitivity runs (BTB 32 to 256 entries, return stack 4 to 16 (no difference), tagless BTB, no late store data, fixed divide cost)

Branch `pipeline` created from `15074b8`. Candidate 0.8.0 written: `rv64_core.sv` replaced by a four-stage single-issue pipeline (F: registered instruction-cache read with fill bypass; D: register read, JAL and backward branches redirect F (1 bubble); E: execute, forwarding from M's integer result and from the last retirement, mispredict redirect (2 bubbles); M: data cache read registered as the instruction enters M, bus access, retirement, traps). Load or multiply result used by the next instruction: 1 clock; store data from a load is taken in M without a stall. A store to the beat of a younger fetched instruction flushes and refetches; traps wait until no fetch is outstanding. Register file has no reset loop; a sequencer zeroes it in 32 clocks after reset. Decode, B, multiply and divide logic reused; ports and trace unchanged (retire2/retire3 stay 0). `test_cpu.py` slot-use checks emptied on this branch (single issue)

Pipeline candidate: compiles with `iverilog -g2012 -Wall` without warnings; regression 55 programs x 3 = 165 runs pass on the first full run with default caches and with 2-line caches; `check_bitmanip.py` passes. Unlogged Dhrystone (`rv64imb`, reference runtime): **0.7944 DMIPS/MHz**, about 716 clocks per run (0.7.1: 2.2163). Better than the model's 0.700 for static prediction because this design's redirects cost 1 and 2 bubbles, not 2 and 3

ECP5 runs started for the pipeline candidate (snapshot `build/cpu/synth/p080a.sv`): 4-line caches, and default 512-line caches to check block-RAM inference. The 0.7.0 and 0.7.1 runs are still in Yosys after 42 minutes

Pipeline candidate with a branch target buffer (64 entries, direct-mapped on pc[7:2], 10-bit partial tags, 2-bit counters, a return flag) read in F, and a 4-entry return-address stack updated in E; D's static prediction is kept for BTB misses. Regression 165/165 with default and 2-line caches. Unlogged Dhrystone (`rv64imb`, reference): **0.9216 DMIPS/MHz**, about 618 clocks per run (+16% over 0.7944; model 0.890 with 3-bubble redirects)

Yosys `synth_ecp5` of the first pipeline candidate (no BTB): 4-line caches 15,171 LUT4, 1,323 CCU2C, 141 TRELLIS_DPR16X4 (register file in LUT RAM), 16 MULT18X18D, 1,985 flip-flops (0.3.0: 22,887 LUT4, 3,662 flip-flops); default 512-line caches add 10 DP16KD block RAMs (caches inferred as block RAM), 19,844 LUT4, 3,104 flip-flops. Place and route running
Commit `ba38182` on branch `pipeline`: pipeline candidate with BTB, and the pipeline model (not versioned; local only)

Return stack moved from E to D (calls push and returns pop as they leave D; a return in F can take the target of a call leaving D in the same clock). Regression 165/165 (default and 2-line caches). Unlogged Dhrystone: 0.9216 DMIPS/MHz, unchanged: the remaining JALR misses are not return-stack timing (the model attributes them to BTB conflicts)

ECP5 place and route of the first pipeline candidate (`p080a`, no BTB; LFE5U-85F speed 6, seed 1): **21.09 MHz** with 512-line caches (23,072 of 83,640 cells; critical path 47.4 ns, 16.5 ns logic, 30.9 ns routing) and **19.87 MHz** with 4-line caches (18,861 cells; 17.4 ns logic, 32.9 ns routing). No faster than 0.3.0 (22.49 MHz): the critical path runs from M's exception flag through the stall logic and E's operand forwarding into the divider's set-up (operand magnitudes, leading-zero counts, early results) and on to M's result register

Divider set-up moved from E to M: divide operands are registered as the instruction enters M; M's first clock completes the early cases or sets up the loop. E's result for multiply and divide is now 0. Regression 165/165 (default and 2-line caches); unlogged Dhrystone 0.9202 DMIPS/MHz (one more clock per divide). ECP5 runs of the BTB version (`p080b`) were stopped as superseded; `p080c` (this version, 512-line caches) started at 00:31:17

256-entry BTB tried in simulation: 0.9670 DMIPS/MHz (+5% over 64 entries, as the model predicted from conflict misses); kept, with only target bits 31:2 stored (upper bits from the PC; a target in another 4 GiB region is mispredicted and corrected in E). Regression 165/165 with default and 2-line caches; Dhrystone 0.9670 unchanged by the compression

On request, work moved back to `main`: the uncommitted pipeline changes were stashed, `main` fast-forwarded from `15074b8` to the branch's one commit `ba38182`, and the stash restored. `origin/main` was already at `15074b8`, pushed from outside this session. Then, on `main`: the pipelined core moved to its own file `rtl/cpu/rv64_pipe.sv` and `rtl/cpu/rv64_core.sv` restored byte for byte to 0.7.1 (SHA-256 `dd153c8d...`), so both implementations are kept. `test_cpu.py`, `check_bitmanip.py`, `run_bench.py` and `run_dhrystone.ps1` take `--core multicycle|pipe` (default multicycle); pipe runs use build folders and records ending in `-pipe`, and run logs and trends keep the two cores apart
Both cores, regression 55 programs x 3 = 165 runs with default and 2-line caches, and `check_bitmanip.py`: all pass (`build/cpu/regress_both.sh`)
`origin/main` found at `ba38182`: the pipeline commit had been pushed from outside this session's commands after the fast-forward

Recorded as architecture 0.8.0 (MINOR: a second implementation whose instruction fetches are speculative, visible on the bus; ISA, ports and trace unchanged). `cpu/architecture.md` describes the pipelined implementation
Commit `53c6772`, both cores on `main` (0.8.0); tagged `cpu-v0.8.0`
Logged runs, pipelined core (`--core pipe`, `-Record`): `rv64imb` reference **0.9670 DMIPS/MHz**, fast runtime **1.1744**; [devlog-53c6772.md](devlog/devlog-53c6772.md)

ECP5 place and route of the pipeline with the divider set-up in M (`p080c`, 64-entry BTB, 512-line caches): **24.30 MHz** (from 21.09), 25,039 cells, 456.5 s; critical path 41.2 ns (12.3 ns logic, 28.9 ns routing) from the data-cache tag block RAM through M's hit check, M's completion, E's and D's advance and the next-fetch-PC select into `f_pc`. The stall decision runs the length of the pipeline in one clock and its enables drive hundreds of flip-flops. Estimate: 0.3.0 21.3 DMIPS (22.49 MHz x 0.9473); this pipeline about 23 DMIPS (24.3 MHz x 0.9670 for the 256-entry BTB, whose own clock is not yet measured). Next: decouple fetch from the stall chain

Candidate 0.8.1, step 1 (`rv64_pipe.sv`): fetch decoupled from the stall chain. A 4-entry fetch queue sits between F and D (D takes F's instruction directly when the queue is empty); F advances whenever the queue is not full, a registered condition. E and D redirects are sent once, as soon as the stage knows, instead of when the stage advances (E waits for valid operands first). Store-to-fetched-beat and `fence.i` flushes are registered and act one clock after the retirement, discarding everything younger, including an instruction that entered M at that edge; the check also covers queue entries. The return stack moved to F (calls and returns update it as they are fetched). Regression (pipe core) 165/165 with default and 2-line caches; Dhrystone 0.9670, unchanged. A first attempt to start its ECP5 run died silently: a background job started from a WSL command that exited at once did not survive; later jobs wait a few seconds before the command exits

Step 2: X stage. M finishes its instruction in one clock without waiting: it retires it (integer result, load hit, multiply, or a bus access completed in that clock) or hands an unfinished bus access to X, which holds the identical request until the bus completes and then retires it; M waits while X is busy. So whether E may advance depends only on registers (X busy, divide still running), not on the data-cache hit; a bus error in M's first clock traps from X one clock later. Divides always take their set-up clock. X's data-cache write also updates the line M already read. Regression 165/165 (default and 2-line caches), B cross-check passes, Dhrystone 0.9670

ECP5 result for the tagged 0.8.0 pipelined core (`p080d`, 512-line caches): **28.00 MHz**, 27,495 cells, 348.1 s; critical path 35.7 ns (13.8 ns logic, 21.9 ns routing) from E's instruction through operand forwarding, the load/store misalignment check, E's exception flag and E's mispredict redirect into the next-fetch-PC select and the instruction-cache block-RAM address. About 27 DMIPS (28.0 x 0.9670) against about 21 for 0.3.0: the first absolute gain

Step 3: redirect checks split between D and E. D compares fetch's prediction with what it can compute itself (JAL target; conditional-branch target with the BTB's direction, or taken if backward without a BTB entry; fall-through for anything else; JALR keeps the prediction) and redirects once on a mismatch. E checks only a conditional branch's direction and a JALR's target, and no longer waits for its exception flag (a faulting instruction traps in M either way). Regression 165/165 (default and 2-line caches), B cross-check passes, Dhrystone 0.9670. ECP5 runs of steps 1, 2 and 3 (`p081a`, `p081b`, `p081c`) started

ECP5 result for step 1 alone (`p081a`): **25.67 MHz**, 28,026 cells, critical path 39.0 ns (9.1 ns logic, 29.9 ns routing), slower than 0.8.0's 28.00. The path runs from the data-cache tag through M's hit check and "M needs the bus" into bus arbitration (a fetch waits for a data access), fetch completion, F's advance and the return-stack enables. Steps 2 and 3 keep that dependency

Step 4: a new fetch no longer waits on whether M needs the bus this clock; it waits whenever M holds a load or store (a registered condition). Regression 165/165 (default and 2-line caches), B cross-check passes, Dhrystone 0.9669 (from 0.9670). ECP5 run `p081d` started

Tried to add a `--noabc9` option to `synth_fmax.py` so the 0.7.x syntheses (in Yosys for 85 minutes) could finish faster: Yosys 0.33 rejected it, because in 0.33 `synth_ecp5` already maps with ABC by default and ABC9 is the opt-in. Option removed; reports now name the mapper
Commit `251ac29`, pipelined core restructured for clock rate (0.8.1); tagged `cpu-v0.8.1`, local only

ECP5 results for the 0.8.1 steps (512-line caches): step 2 `p081b` (fetch queue and X stage) **24.85 MHz**, 41,002 cells, critical path 40.3 ns (8.9 logic, 31.4 routing) from E's instruction through the E redirect into the return-stack enables; step 4 `p081d` (= tagged 0.8.1) **28.29 MHz**, 41,178 cells, 35.3 ns (7.6 logic, 27.7 routing). 0.8.1 is only 1% faster than 0.8.0 (28.00 MHz) and 50% larger: the logic on the longest path fell from 13.8 to 7.6 ns but routing stayed near 28 ns. Step 3 `p081c` still routing
New user direction: move toward the Apple M5 (an out-of-order design). Plan: a third implementation, `rtl/cpu/rv64_ooo.sv`, built in stages that each pass the full trace regression

Out-of-order model added to `sim/cpu/bench/pipeline_model.py` by a side agent (`--ooo`; Python 3.12.10; in-order output unchanged, checked with `cmp`). Caches always hit; ordering (a) loads wait for older stores to retire, (b) loads never wait (an upper bound), (c) loads wait for older stores to issue (store-queue forwarding). `rv64imb` reference trace, DMIPS/MHz: in-order w1 BTB256 0.961, w2 1.361; out-of-order 1-wide (a) 0.954 to 0.972; **2-wide, ROB 32, IQ 16, 2 ALUs, 1 memory port, checkpoint recovery: (a) 1.443, (c) 1.733, (b) 1.749**; 4-wide ROB 64 3 ALUs (b) 2.428. Memory ordering is the largest lever ((a) to (c) +20%), then width; under (a) a load latency of 3 instead of 2 costs 15%; recovery (retire, early, checkpoint) is worth 3% here and 9% on the fast-runtime trace. Limits: no cache misses, no wrong-path occupancy, no clock-rate dimension

Stage A written (`rtl/cpu/rv64_ooo.sv`, 1,011 lines): the pipelined core's front end; rename of one instruction per clock onto 64 physical registers; 32-entry reorder buffer retiring one per clock; 8-entry issue queue with wakeup and select; an integer port (multiply/divide unit behind it) and a two-stage load/store port; stores write at retirement; loads issue when every older store has retired; mispredict redirects fetch at execute and rename waits for the branch to retire. Decode, B and M logic reused from the pipelined core. `--core ooo` added to `test_cpu.py`, `check_bitmanip.py`, `run_bench.py`, `run_dhrystone.ps1` and the run log

First regression of stage A: 53 of 55 programs pass; `memory_lanes` and `mul_then_store_pad0` fail at 19 wait cycles with "unstable stalled request". A debug bench (`build/cpu/ooo-debug/`) showed a load miss's held request dropped: completing a store in the load/store port's first stage also cleared its second stage. Fixed; that exposed hangs in three programs: when the first stage finished a store in the same clock the second finished a load, the second stage was not cleared, and the finished load later read an unwritten cache tag (X). Fixed by handling the two cases separately

Stage A: regression 165/165 with default and 2-line caches; `check_bitmanip.py --core ooo` passes. Unlogged Dhrystone (`rv64imb`, reference): **0.7888 DMIPS/MHz**, below the pipelined core's 0.9670 and the model's 1-wide (a) 0.954: this design's load-to-dependent latency is 3 clocks and loads wait for older stores to retire
Logged runs, out-of-order core (`-Core ooo -Record`): `rv64imb` reference 0.7888 DMIPS/MHz, fast runtime 0.9306; [devlog-251ac29.md](devlog/devlog-251ac29.md). ECP5 run of stage A (`o090`) started
Commit `f1f94c4`, out-of-order stage A (0.9.0); tagged `cpu-v0.9.0`, local only

0.9.1 written (out-of-order core): a load issues once every older store has its address and data; in its second stage it scans the older stores still in the reorder buffer for its 8-byte beat and takes the youngest one's data when it covers every byte the load reads; on a partial overlap it waits for those stores to retire and reads the bus. A store retiring in the clock a load reads the cache passes its bytes into that read. Regression 165/165 with default and 2-line caches; B cross-check passes. Unlogged Dhrystone 0.9428 DMIPS/MHz (from 0.7888, +19.5%; the model predicted about +20% for this ordering change)

New test `store_load_forwarding` (full, partial, narrower and wider overlaps, the younger of two stores, a dependent chain; run twice): all three cores pass, 56 programs x 3 = 168 runs each, and the out-of-order core with 2-line caches. Mutation check: with forwarding disabled in the out-of-order core, 5 programs fail including the new test; the RTL was restored and checked
Logged runs, out-of-order 0.9.1 (`-Core ooo -Record`): `rv64imb` reference **0.9428 DMIPS/MHz**, fast runtime **1.0684**; [devlog-f1f94c4.md](devlog/devlog-f1f94c4.md)
Commit `7bf8f3d`, store-to-load forwarding (0.9.1); tagged `cpu-v0.9.1`, local only

0.9.2 written: the out-of-order core made two-wide (body rewritten, 1,280 lines): two-instruction fetch from an aligned beat with a second BTB lookup (none after a predicted-taken transfer, call or return), 8-entry fetch queue without the F-to-D bypass, two D slots each checking its prediction, rename and dispatch of two per clock (the second may read the first's result), a second integer port using the multicycle core's `simple_alu` for simple integer and B operations, retirement of two per clock (the second never a store, `fence.i`, mispredicted branch or trap, and not two control transfers at once)

First run: 55 of 56 programs pass; `store_load_forwarding` hung. The load/store port's second stage held a load waiting (partial overlap) for older stores to retire, while an older memory instruction at the ROB head, still in the issue queue, could not enter the port. Fixed by issuing memory instructions in program order (the port takes the oldest one, when ready)

0.9.2: regression 168/168 with default and 2-line caches; B cross-check passes. Unlogged Dhrystone (`rv64imb`, reference): **1.2768 DMIPS/MHz** (from 0.9428, +35%). The model's point for this width (ROB 32, IQ 16, 2 ALUs, checkpoint recovery, store-queue ordering, load latency 2) is 1.733; this design has IQ 8, load latency 3, no checkpoint recovery, in-order memory issue and one more front-end stage
Logged runs, out-of-order 0.9.2: `rv64imb` reference **1.2768 DMIPS/MHz**, fast runtime **1.4419**; [devlog-7bf8f3d.md](devlog/devlog-7bf8f3d.md)

ECP5 run of out-of-order stage A (0.9.0, 512-line caches): **does not fit**. Yosys maps it to 107,072 LUT4 (part: 83,640), 31,302 PFUMX, 13,414 L6MUX21, 17,976 flip-flops, 2,133 CCU2C, 388 DPR16X4, 12 DP16KD, 16 MULT18X18D (624.6 s); nextpnr: "Unable to find legal placement for all cells, design is probably at utilisation limit" (1,212.6 s in all). The physical register file and the reorder-buffer fields are flip-flops with many read and write ports. The out-of-order results so far are simulation results only; fitting the design is a separate task
Commit `11acc17`, two-wide out-of-order core (0.9.2); tagged `cpu-v0.9.2`, local only
A 16-entry issue queue tried: 1.2913 DMIPS/MHz (+1.1%, as the model predicted); not kept, because the design already does not fit and the queue's area doubles. Index widths now follow `IQ_N`

Stall statistics for the two-wide core on Dhrystone (debug bench `build/cpu/ooo-debug/tb_ostat.sv`, timed region, 222,875 clocks): retire 2 in 50% of clocks, 1 in 23%, none in 27%; issue queue with fewer than two free slots in 43%; a store waiting at the head in 9% (all of it the one-clock-ahead tag read not ready: 20,525 clocks); oldest memory instruction not ready in 38%; memory port used in 45%

Pending store update: a retiring store writes the bus at once; its data-cache update and instruction-cache invalidation follow one clock later from a register (loads reading that line merge it; fetch treats that index as a miss for that clock). Store wait at the head fell to 11 clocks but Dhrystone stayed at 1.2768: the head now waited for unfinished instructions instead (56,197 clocks, half of them loads). The single in-order memory port is the limit

Stores split into address and data: a store issues once its address is known and reads its data register at retirement; forwarding reads that register and waits until it is written; loads wait only for older store addresses. Regression 168/168 (default and 2-line caches), B cross-check passes

WSL crashed during the next run (`Wsl/Service/E_UNEXPECTED`), most likely from memory pressure: several Yosys syntheses (the area study and the 0.7.x ECP5 runs) were running at once on the 15 GB VM. The 0.7.0/0.7.1 ECP5 job (in Yosys since 23:36) ended with exit code 15 and never produced a result; the area study's runs were lost. WSL restarted with `wsl --shutdown`; agents told to run at most two syntheses at a time

Dhrystone on the split-store core: reference runtime 1.5648 DMIPS/MHz (from 1.2768, +22.6%) with all checks passing; a logged reference run at 02:54:13 used this RTL. The fast-runtime run then failed its differential check at event 8169 (`lw` at 0xa34 read 0xb, reference 0xc). A cache-line watch (`tb_dbg3.sv`) showed the cause: the data-cache write was `if (fill) ... else if (pending store)`, so a fill to any other line in the same clock dropped the store's update. Fixed so both write (the store's update is skipped only for a fill to its own line). Also changed: a load that waited in its second stage reads the bus afterwards
After a session restart: regression 168/168 (default and 2-line caches), B cross-check passes; the 0.9.3 history row and rubric hashes were re-recorded for the fixed RTL

Logged runs, out-of-order 0.9.3: `rv64imb` reference **1.5648 DMIPS/MHz**, fast runtime **1.5777**; [devlog-11acc17.md](devlog/devlog-11acc17.md). (The 02:54:13 reference row in the run index is the same result on the RTL before the fill fix)
Commit `8f207a0`, split stores and deferred store cache update (0.9.3); tagged `cpu-v0.9.3`, local only

Stall statistics on 0.9.3 (181,861 clocks): retire 2 in 62% of clocks, 1 in 28%, none in 11%; rename 2 in 65%; fetch delivered about 1.63 instructions per clock (two only from the start of a beat); memory port used in 55%

0.9.4: fetch also reads the next beat, so the second instruction can come from it. Regression 168/168 (default and 2-line caches). Dhrystone `rv64imb` reference 1.5778 DMIPS/MHz (+0.8%), fast runtime 1.6180 (+2.6%): two-wide rename and retirement are now the ceiling
Logged runs, out-of-order 0.9.4: reference **1.5778**, fast runtime **1.6180**; [devlog-8f207a0.md](devlog/devlog-8f207a0.md)

User direction: size the core after the Apple M5 (FPGA fit later) and raise IPC. M5 P-core figures from the one independent study (useless-husband/m5-uarch): 10 NOPs per clock, 8 integer ALUs, 3 multipliers, 3 loads and 2 stores per clock, 2 taken branches per clock, about 1,334 instructions in flight for an ordinary mix, 396 integer rename registers, L1I 192 KiB, L1D 128 KiB, 3-clock load-to-use, 16.7-clock mispredict
Commit `af0a3a1`, cross-beat fetch (0.9.4); tagged `cpu-v0.9.4`, local only

M5 detail from the study's results file (`results/apple-m5/apple-m5.json`, read by a side agent): integer add 1 clock at 6.7 to 7.7 per clock; multiply 3 per clock, 3 clocks; divide 0.5 per clock, 7 clocks; loads 3 per clock, 3 clocks (pointer chase); stores 2 per clock; branches 3 not-taken or 2 taken per clock; store queue 137, load queue 486, unresolved branches 194; move elimination at rename; store-to-load forwarding as low as 0.66 clocks (no explanation given); constant-value load prediction (P core only). Ranked proposals: (1) 2-way 16-32 KiB I-cache with multi-beat lines; (2) pipelined or burst bus reads (SoC contract change); (3) 32-64 B D-cache lines with burst fill; (4) multiply latency 3 to 2; (5) global-history direction predictor (trace estimate compress 12.1 to 7.2 MPKI); (6) several misses in flight (naive version livelocks). **FFmpeg decisions** (coordinator, on `build/research/ffmpeg.md`; FFmpeg n9.1 = 74e43935, LGPL/GPL, kept out of the repository). Of 647 RISC-V entry points, vector step 1 can run 20 (3%) and the full RVV-CONTRACT 97 (15%). The rest need widening (423), fixed point with vxrm (377), narrowing (155) or segments (105). The step-1 vector unit drains the ROB on every vector instruction and moves one element per clock, so it will likely be slower than scalar C on streaming kernels until the pipelined, beat-wide vector unit lands; that unit is the precondition for any FFmpeg gain. No A or Zicond is needed except for threading. Proposed `--benchmark ff` (part A, about 14 FFmpeg DSP kernels driven the way checkasm drives them; part B, an H.264 CABAC decode of a generated QCIF clip, FLAC, then dav1d) is noted for later and not started. Integer-vector, widening/narrowing, fixed-point and segment MINORs are confirmed as the vector roadmap after 0.18.0.

**RV64GC + privilege + MMU research for Linux** (research agent, web only, nothing built or downloaded; `build/research/rv64gc-linux.md`). Linux needs `rv64ima`: the kernel's -march starts with rv64ima, C and F/D are kernel options, OpenSBI needs rv64ima_zicsr and emulates AMOs over LR/SC and a missing `time` CSR, and Sv39 alone suffices. RV64GC matters for distro binaries, V8 and Node, not for booting. In piece 113, 150,003 of 150,001 window retirements are in lzma_crc_update (0xbd2c-0xc214); the counter includes the window-edge instruction. Pieces 116 and 119 also resume there. **Full RVV research report** (Sonnet research agent; build/research/rvv-complete.md, static scripts in build/research/rvv-complete/). In the RTL, RV64_OOO_V executes vset*, the vector CSRs, ld/st and FP32 arithmetic. Every integer, mask, permute, reduction, indexed and segment instruction, and every FP SEW other than 32, raises cause 2. The contract and vec_ref.py already define the integer, mask, permute, reduction and indexed groups. rv_iss.c has no vector support. Static counts, clang 23.1.5 -O2 -march=rv64gcv on our bench sources: 3,245 vector instructions over 116 mnemonics; only 157 of the 460 functions with vector code would run on step 1. The top blockers are vmv.v.*/vmerge (258 functions), vector-scalar moves (60), extends (46) and the integer ALU (42). RVA23 mandates V, Zvfhmin, Zvbb and Zvkt. Zvkt requires data-independent latency in the integer vector pipes, so there must be no value prediction or early-out there. Recommended order after 2a: 2b (integer ALU, vmv/vmerge, compare, mask, extends, scalar moves); 2c (mul, div, slides, vrgather, vcompress, reductions, with a DIEL timing test from here on); 2d (indexed); then widening, Zvbb, fixed point, segments, FP64, Zvfhmin and the VS state. Coordinator decisions: (a) executing an instruction that used to raise cause 2 changes the ISA the core implements, so each coverage step is a MINOR, even when the contract already defines it, and 2a stays a PATCH; (b) the RTL lockstep oracle for vector work is a vector mode in rv_iss, carried over from build/cpu/fp/rv_iss_fp.c with provenance, with Spike as the independent second oracle, and both go on the docket before 2b; (c) 2b-2d are re-scoped against the real 2a RTL once it lands, and the opcode count is re-run dynamically then.

days.title: setup, review rubric, roadmap and first benchmark
findings: **The local toolchain did not match the docs.** The README and quick start say Ubuntu 24.04 under WSL with Icarus is already installed. On this ARM64 Windows workstation WSL 2.7.10 was present but had no distribution. Installed Ubuntu 24.04, Icarus Verilog 12.0 and Python 3.12.3. Windows has Python 3.12.10 (ARM64) and LLVM 23.1.5.

**The core passes its own tests.** The main regression passed 96 of 96 differential runs plus the reset and RAM-wrapper checks, in about 12 seconds. The historical PicoRV32 smoke test passed in 26 cycles.

**GitHub Pages is not enabled for the repository.** The Pages API returns 404 and there is no Pages branch or workflow. The project's pages (CPU visualizer and core explainer) are served locally by `sim/cpu/serve_visualizer.py`.

**Building the visualizer lessons rewrites two tracked files.** `cpu/programs-verification.json` and `cpu/visualizer-verification.json` change on every lesson build, and again when **Run simulation** is clicked in the viewer. Both are modified and uncommitted; the decision is tracked in [TODO.md](TODO.md).

**The core cannot yet be called "good" or "performant".** A review rubric was written ([cpu/review-rubric.md](cpu/review-rubric.md)). The author's gate reading at commit `0483d99`: external-model check, lint and synthesis, known-issue list and independent review are not met, and no performance gate can be met without synthesis or a board.

**V8 is not a usable benchmark.** It needs an operating system, an MMU, RV64GC-class hardware and hundreds of megabytes of memory, and would take many hours per billion instructions in RTL simulation. Chosen instead: CoreMark (primary) and Dhrystone (secondary), with the riscv-tests benchmark programs as the next small set.
**RISC-V has a ratified vector extension but no ratified matrix extension** (as of mid-2026). Integrated (IME) and attached (AME) matrix approaches are recorded as research in the to-do list.

**The core has no caches.** Main memory is a 16 KiB RAM that answers in one clock, so caches cannot speed up today's simulation. A staged plan (slow memory model, then L1, then L2, measured at each step) is in the to-do list.
**Dhrystone runs on the unchanged core: 0.260 DMIPS/MHz** in simulation (non-compliant run, rubric evidence class E1). Details below.

**Benchmark scores depend heavily on the compiler.** The same Dhrystone source scores 0.260 DMIPS/MHz with clang 23.1.5, 0.249 with clang 21.1.6 (the CI runner) and 0.217 with Ubuntu's clang 18.1.3. All three pass every check.

**Clocks per instruction follow from the memory timing.** The RAM acknowledges one clock after each request, so a fetch takes 2 clocks and execution 1. Most instructions take 3 clocks; loads and stores take 5. Dhrystone averages 3.65; the earlier C demo, with fewer memory operations, averages about 3.05.

**The simulator is faster than first estimated.** The C demo record implies about 17,000 instructions per second. The Dhrystone timing run retired 307,336 instructions over 1,120,105 clocks in 9.0 seconds: about 34,000 instructions or 124,000 clocks per second, including process start-up.
**This LLVM installation has no RISC-V runtime library.** Bare-metal programs that multiply or divide need their own helper routines; the benchmark runtime now provides them.

**Existing verification records contain local user paths.** `cpu/verification.json` and `cpu/c-demo-results.json` include absolute paths from the machine that produced them. The new Dhrystone record stores repository-relative paths instead. The older records are unchanged.
**The repository check script could not be run locally** in this session because the assistant's permission settings blocked it. CI runs it on every push, and it passed for each commit below.

**First rubric scorecard: 37.1 of 100, the lowest ("foundation") band, no claims granted.** Strongest: traps and reset (R2) and reproducibility (R9), both 62%. Weakest: FPGA implementation (R5) at 0%, performance (R4) at 22% and verification depth (R3) at 25%. It is an automated self-assessment, recomputed on every Dhrystone run from `cpu/rubric-evidence.json`.

**Correction to the rubric's section 11 reading.** That reading listed HG1 (scope label) as met, but the scope label has no performance target, which rubric section 2 requires. The evidence file records HG1 as not met until a target is declared. Section 11 is left as written, since it is a dated reading.

**The CPU architecture is now versioned: 0.1.0.** The unchanged C0 core, called "revision 0" until now, becomes 0.1.0. Before 1.0.0, MINOR changes for any change to the architectural contract and PATCH for any other RTL change. Proposed criteria for 1.0.0: C1 complete, an external-model check (rubric HG3) and a first exact-part synthesis. Rules and history: [cpu/architecture.md](cpu/architecture.md) section 9.

**Profile of Dhrystone: fetching is 54.8% of all clocks.** Each instruction spends 2 clocks being fetched and 1 executing; loads and stores add 2. The per-instruction clock model reproduces the measured timed region exactly (1,094,103 clocks); the whole-program counts differ by 3 clocks, the final `ebreak`.

**The byte-at-a-time string routines dominate.** `strcpy` and `strcmp` from `sim/cpu/bench/runtime.c` execute 47% of all instructions (281 of 600 per run). Software divide is only 5% of clocks (one `__divdi3` call per run); multiplication never reaches `__muldi3` because the compiler uses shifts. This corrects advice given earlier in the session that hardware multiply and divide would be the biggest gain for Dhrystone: the profile estimates only 1.05x.

**40% of instructions could reuse the previous fetch.** 241 of 600 instructions per run are the second half of an 8-byte fetch beat that was just read. Model estimates: a one-entry fetch buffer gives 1.12x to 1.28x (2,188 down to 1,947 or 1,706 clocks per run); an ideal pipeline gives at most 3.65x. These are estimates from the trace, not measured RTL.
**Run logs are now split by commit.** The two runs previously logged at the end of this file were moved unchanged to [devlog/devlog-3110337.md](devlog/devlog-3110337.md).

**The optimization loop took Dhrystone from 2,188.2 to 555.7 clocks per run, 3.94x** (0.260 to 1.024 DMIPS/MHz, simulation). Order of gains: instruction fetch first (fetch buffer 1.28x, then a 4 KiB instruction cache 1.73x), then memory waits (early issue 1.24x, same-clock writes 1.11x, a data cache 1.20x), then instruction count (M, 1.08x on the `rv64im` build).

**The loop stopped at about one instruction per clock.** On 0.4.0 only 2.6 of 555.7 clocks per run are not instruction execution: two divide steps, 0.6 fetch and 0.1 memory. Lower needs fewer instructions (compiler or runtime, not the core) or more than one instruction per clock (a superscalar redesign, not a refinement).

**The gains depend on assumptions not yet tested.** Both 4 KiB caches hold all of Dhrystone, and the RAM answers in one clock. The cache lookups use the just-computed next PC and data address in the same clock, which may lower the clock frequency; nothing has been synthesized. A slow-memory model and a first synthesis are the checks that matter next.

**Two tooling problems found and fixed during the loop.** The visualizer testbench detected writes in a way that stopped working at 0.2.2. The profiler's "issue loads and stores in EXECUTE" estimate overstated the gain for 0.3.0 and 0.4.0; the run logs [devlog-90ee1ea.md](devlog/devlog-90ee1ea.md) and [devlog-88db627.md](devlog/devlog-88db627.md) still show the old figure and are left as written.

**The core contract changed in three MINOR steps.** `ICACHE_BEATS` (0.2.0) and `DCACHE_BEATS` (0.3.0) are new parameters, every address is now treated as cacheable, and 0.4.0 adds M. Each version has a history row in [cpu/architecture.md](cpu/architecture.md) and a local `cpu-vX.Y.Z` tag.

Commit `241a9af`, second-slot stores and forwarding (0.5.4); tagged `cpu-v0.5.4`. Runs: `rv64im` reference 335.8 clocks per run, 1.6951 DMIPS/MHz; fast runtime 269.9, 2.1091 (first build past 2 DMIPS/MHz); `rv64i` reference 358.8, 1.5861; [devlog-241a9af.md](devlog/devlog-241a9af.md)

Blockers on 0.5.4: fast runtime issues 413.8 of 470.1 instructions per run in pairs (2-wide floor about 235 clocks); remaining: JALR first 18.0, taken branch first 15.0, store second 10.1 clocks per run. Reference runtime: taken branch first 55.0, load-to-branch dependency 23.0, JALR first 20.0

0.5.5 branch folding written. Regression 135/135 passed, but the visualizer lesson build failed: when a fetch completed, the next instruction was captured from `pc2`, which since 0.5.5 is the folding target computed from the stale previous instruction. In the lesson it captured `j .` from 0x10 instead of the instruction at 0x30. Fixed (use pc+4 in FETCH). New test `fetch_after_stale_jump` reproduces it: with the bug put back it fails (x5 = 7 at 0x30 instead of x7 = 2); with the fix it passes. Regression 138/138 with default and 2-line caches; all lessons verify; C demo 11,568 clocks. Lesson rebuilds are now part of every step

Commit `5f1f6b1`, branch folding (0.5.5); tagged `cpu-v0.5.5`. Runs: `rv64im` reference 287.8 clocks per run, 1.9777 DMIPS/MHz (7.60x over 0.1.0); fast runtime 251.9, 2.2598; `rv64i` reference 308.9, 1.8428; [devlog-5f1f6b1.md](devlog/devlog-5f1f6b1.md)

Second issue model, with folding, forwarding depth and port limits, calibrated against 0.5.5 (287.0 modelled against 287.8 measured, reference runtime). 3-wide with one level of forwarding: 213 clocks per run reference (2.67 DMIPS/MHz), 182 fast (3.13). 4-wide with two taken branches and three levels of forwarding: 144 reference (3.95), 123 fast (4.63). 8-wide with forwarding chains of seven: 73 and 63 (7.8 and 9.0)

Caution recorded: forwarding chains raise DMIPS/MHz by doing more work per clock, which lengthens the clock; at the extreme a whole program fits in one very long clock. DMIPS/MHz gains from deeper logic are not real performance unless synthesis shows the clock survives. Decided to measure logic depth before going wider
Yosys 0.33 installed in Ubuntu; `sim/cpu/synth_depth.py` written to map the core to 6-input LUTs and report the longest path in LUT levels

First depth synthesis of 0.5.5 stopped after a long run without finishing: the 0.4.0 multiply logic built three 128x128-bit products. Replaced by one signed 65x65 product with a sign or zero bit per operand (same results; M tests pass). Depth synthesis restarted in the background

0.6.0 B extension written: one `bitmanip` function used by both slots; encodings taken from LLVM's assembler; reference model extended. New tests: `b_extension` (all 40 instructions over extreme operands) and `random_b_606`/`random_b_707`. Regression 147/147, 106 instruction names, with default and 2-line caches; all seven lessons verify

Independent B check (`sim/cpu/check_bitmanip.py`): the same C built without B and with Zba/Zbb/Zbs gives identical results on the RTL in all 12 groups; the B build uses 28 distinct B instructions; both traces match the reference. Benchmark builds gain `rv64imb` (`rv64im_zba_zbb_zbs_zifencei`), and the fast runtime uses `orc.b` when Zbb is available
Commit `f78d62a`, B extension and single multiplier (0.6.0); tagged `cpu-v0.6.0`, local only

First `rv64imb` run failed a consistency check: timing run and trace disagreed by one instruction on the timed region. Both retire the same instructions in the same order; the difference is at the region's edges, where a marker store can retire in the same clock as the next instruction. The runner now requires exact totals, allows the region edges to differ by up to two, and takes the region's instruction count from the trace in program order. Earlier results are unaffected (their counts matched exactly)

0.6.0 runs: `rv64imb` reference 285.8 clocks per run, 1.9916 DMIPS/MHz; `rv64imb` fast 247.8, 2.2964; `rv64im` reference unchanged 287.8; `rv64im` fast unchanged 251.9; [devlog-f78d62a.md](devlog/devlog-f78d62a.md). B gains 0.7% (reference) and 1.6% (fast), as the static check predicted
Depth synthesis of 0.6.0 completed but recorded nothing: Yosys quiet mode hid the reports. The script now saves them to files; 0.3.0 and 0.6.0 are being measured
Commit `c281389`: 0.6.0 benchmark records and runner fix

Third-slot sizing on the 0.6.0 streams (issue model, calibrated on the measured 2-wide results): an ALU-only third slot that never uses the second slot's result saves about 12% (reference) to 16% (fast); a direct count of ALU instructions issued alone suggested zero, because the gain comes from regrouping, not from single issues

0.7.0 third slot written, with a third retirement port carried through the RAM wrapper, testbenches and visualizer. New test `triple_issue` (forwarding from slot one, a third that depends on the second, three writes to one register). Regression 150/150 with default and 2-line caches; B cross-check passes; all lessons verify; C demo 8,756 clocks

Commit `a6e3f87`, third issue slot (0.7.0); tagged `cpu-v0.7.0`. Runs: `rv64imb` reference 256.8 clocks per run, CPI 0.467, 2.2163 DMIPS/MHz (8.52x over 0.1.0); `rv64imb` fast 216.9, 2.6243; `rv64im` reference 258.8, 2.1991; [devlog-a6e3f87.md](devlog/devlog-a6e3f87.md)

First logic-depth results (generic Yosys + ABC, 6-input LUTs, 4-line caches): 0.3.0 has a longest path of 30 LUT levels, 6,309 LUTs, 3,662 flip-flops; the run started on 0.6.0 reports 78 levels, 33,046 LUTs, 4,250 flip-flops. That report was stamped "0.7.0" because the script read the version and hash at the end, after the working copy had moved on; the RTL it synthesized was read at the start (0.6.0). The script now snapshots and hashes its source first

Finding: depth grew 2.6x from 0.3.0 while DMIPS/MHz grew about 2.1x. If clock frequency fell in proportion to depth, absolute performance would not have improved. Three variants of 0.7.0 are being synthesized (as built, multiplier removed, multiplier removed with forwarding and folding off) to find what the deep path is

Both syntheses contain only flip-flops and LUTs: no latches (part of rubric gate HG7; a dedicated lint run is still missing). Size note: up to three instructions per clock needs six register-file read ports and three write ports, which an FPGA builds from flip-flops and wide multiplexers rather than LUT RAM; LUTs grew from 6,309 to 33,046
First variant-synthesis attempt did nothing: PowerShell passed an escaped shell variable through literally. Rerun from a script file

Candidate 0.7.1, registered multiplier: operands registered in EXECUTE, product taken in a new MULTIPLY state one clock later. Regression 150/150 with default and 2-line caches; B cross-check passes. Unlogged Dhrystone run (`rv64imb`, reference runtime): unchanged 256.8 clocks per run, because this build never multiplies at run time

Correction to earlier rows: from "before 21:57" to "23:28 to 23:32", 41 rows had estimated times 20 to 60 minutes later than the events (some later than the time of writing). They now use the commit author times and the run-table times, or a bound from them

Variant `v070-nomul-nofwd` (0.7.0 with the multiplier removed, and with folding (`control0`) and slot-1-to-slot-2 forwarding (`slot0_forward`) forced off): 40 LUT levels, 28,149 LUTs, 4,483 flip-flops, 442.4 s. Its longest path runs from the register file through about 20 single-LUT steps in a row, the pattern of a 64-bit adder carry built from generic LUTs. A generic LUT mapping has no carry chain, so LUT levels overstate adder delay compared with an FPGA, which has dedicated carry logic

`nextpnr-ecp5` 0.6-3build5 (arm64) installed in Ubuntu with `apt-get install nextpnr-ecp5`, to get post-route clock estimates on a real FPGA family (Lattice ECP5) instead of LUT levels. New script `sim/cpu/synth_fmax.py` (Yosys `synth_ecp5`, then nextpnr out of context, 4-line caches); first runs on 0.3.0, 0.7.0 and the 0.7.1 candidate started

Variant results (same flow, 4-line caches, run three at a time): 0.7.0 as built 80 LUT levels, 37,991 LUTs, 4,473 flip-flops, 1,266.6 s; multiplier removed 54 levels, 30,188 LUTs, 1,199.3 s; multiplier removed with folding and forwarding off 40 levels, 28,149 LUTs. The multiplier (a 65x65 product after register read and decode in the same clock) accounts for 26 levels and folding plus slot-1-to-slot-2 forwarding for 14 more. (The 0.7.0 RTL gives 80 levels against the 78 of the 0.6.0 run; ABC results vary a little with the design)

Candidate 0.7.1 (registered multiplier) depth: 52 LUT levels against 80 for 0.7.0, 40,187 LUTs (+2,196, from holding the 130-bit product's operands and selecting its result), 4,606 flip-flops (+133), 1,252.4 s. The deepest path no longer goes through the multiplier: it runs from the register file to a register-file write (the issue and forwarding logic). Adopted as 0.7.1 (PATCH: a multiply takes two clocks and no longer pairs; the ISA and ports do not change). Dhrystone does not multiply at run time, so its clocks do not change (256.8, unlogged run at 23:28 to 23:32)
Commit `129e37e`, registered multiplier (0.7.1); tagged `cpu-v0.7.1`, local only

First ECP5 place and route (0.3.0, LFE5U-85F, CABGA381, speed 6, seed 1, 4-line caches, target 50 MHz): routed, **22.49 MHz** achieved; 23,911 of 83,640 logic cells, 3,662 flip-flops; 945.2 s. Critical path 44.5 ns, of which 9.2 ns logic and 35.3 ns routing: instruction register, load address, data-cache hit, result select, register-file write. nextpnr exits 1 when the target is missed, so the script reported "nextpnr exit 1"; the report was corrected from the log and the script now passes `--timing-allow-fail` and records the critical path

0.7.1 runs: `rv64imb` reference 256.8 clocks per run, 2.2163 DMIPS/MHz (unchanged); `rv64imb` fast 216.9, 2.6243 (unchanged); `rv64im` 261.8, 2.1739 (+3.0 clocks per run against 0.7.0: that build multiplies at run time, and each multiply now takes an extra clock and no longer pairs); `rv64i` 273.9, 2.0780 (first `rv64i` record since 0.5.5's 308.9); [devlog-129e37e.md](devlog/devlog-129e37e.md)

Absolute-performance estimate for 0.3.0: 0.9473 DMIPS/MHz x 22.49 MHz = 21.3 DMIPS on this part (one seed, open timing model, not hardware). The 0.7.0 and 0.7.1 routes are running; their DMIPS/MHz gain (2.34x) is real only if their clock stays above 22.49 / 2.34 = 9.6 MHz
